title: Recommendation and ranking system
summary: Candidate generation, ranking, features and online experiments.
prompt: Design the “recommended for you” feed for a large catalogue (articles, products or videos): pick a few dozen items per user from millions, update with fresh behaviour, and prove with experiments that changes help.

requirements: Functional: return a ranked list of items for a user and context, react to recent clicks within minutes, filter items already seen or unavailable, support A/B tests.
Non-functional: p99 under ~200 ms, millions of users and items, a fallback for brand-new users and items, and an agreed business metric (for example long-term engagement, not just clicks).
estimation: 10M daily users × 5 feed loads = 50M requests a day ≈ 600 per second, ~3k at peak.
Ranking 500 candidates per request at 3k QPS is 1.5M model scores per second, so the ranker must be cheap or batched.
Interaction events: ~1B a day at ~100 bytes ≈ 100 GB a day of logs for training.
api: POST /events {userId, itemId, type: impression|click|dwell|hide, at} into a stream.
Internal: candidates(user, n) per source; features(user, items); score(features).
data: Item catalogue with metadata and availability; item embeddings in an approximate nearest-neighbour index.
Feature store: batch features (user history aggregates) and streaming features (last N clicks), served from a low-latency key-value store and logged at serving time.
Training data: impressions joined to later outcomes, keyed by the features that were actually served.
design: Stage 1, candidate generation: several cheap sources (two-tower embeddings with ANN search, co-visitation, trending, follows) return a few hundred items.
Stage 2, ranking: a model such as gradient-boosted trees or a small network scores each candidate on user, item and context features to predict engagement.
Stage 3, re-ranking: apply business rules, remove seen items, diversify and blend in exploration slots, then cache the page.
Offline: daily training on logged data, evaluation on a later time window, then shadow and A/B tests before full rollout.
deepDives: Metrics: offline NDCG and recall@k guide model choice, but only an online A/B test on the agreed metric decides. Watch guardrail metrics such as hides and latency.
Training-serving skew: log features at serving time and train on those, rather than recomputing them later; leakage from future events inflates offline scores.
Cold start: content features and popularity for new items, onboarding choices and context for new users, plus exploration so new items collect data.
Feedback loops: the model only learns from what it showed. Exploration and position-bias correction keep it from narrowing.
bottlenecks: Ranking cost at peak: cap candidates, batch scoring, and precompute for inactive users.
Feature lookups: fetch all features for a request in one batched call from a co-located store.
Embedding refresh: rebuild the ANN index on a schedule and swap it atomically.
tradeoffs: Precomputed feeds are cheap and fast but stale; online ranking is fresh but costs compute per request. Many systems mix both.
Optimising clicks is easy to measure but rewards clickbait; dwell time or retention is better aligned but slower to observe.
A bigger ranking model may lift offline metrics yet lose online if it adds latency.

rubric.text: Agreed the objective and online success metric.
Split serving into candidate generation, ranking and re-ranking.
Described features from batch and streaming sources.
Kept latency in budget with caching and batched scoring.
Handled cold start for new users and items.
Validated with offline metrics then an online A/B test.
Prevented training-serving skew and leakage by logging served features.
Addressed feedback loops with exploration and position-bias correction.
